title: Load Test One Endpoint, Watch the Rest
summary: Load test one endpoint while keeping another steady. See how separate schedules and latency goals reveal slowdowns an overall average can hide.
body_markdown:
Suppose you run a banking app. Month-end is coming, and customers are pulling statements. You want to load test the statement endpoint, but the question you need answered is: can people still post transactions while that’s happening?


Turning up every request in a recording makes that harder to answer. You’ve increased both workloads, and their combined average latency can hide a slowdown in the one you care about.


I’d rather increase statement traffic, keep transaction posting steady, and measure posting on its own. That’s what endpoint and session load plans let you do. Check the[compatibility and release notes](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/replay/endpoint-session-load-plans/) first: use matching CLI, generator, operator, and cloud components, and verify the available cluster launch path in your installation.


🎯 Key Takeaways


- Give each endpoint or user journey its own schedule so you can see how one affects another.
- Check the endpoint that matters during the busiest part of the test. Require enough samples to trust the result.
- A mock can make a dependency predictable without making it faster. Ours was 2.6% slower than a fast local dependency in[30 matched runs](https://speedscale.com/resources/load-plan-measurements/real-vs-mock-30-pairs.json) .


## Give each workload its own schedule


In Speedscale, you use a filter to select recorded traffic and put it in a load group. That group can contain one endpoint, several endpoints, or complete user journeys. Each gets its own schedule and goals.


For the banking example, I’d put statements in one group and transaction posting in another. Then I can ramp up statements while sending posting requests at a steady rate.


This screenshot uses our storefront demo. The product page requests have their own schedule, just as statement requests would in the banking app.


The scheduling choice matters. **Arrivals** start requests or journeys at a set rate, even when the app slows down. **Concurrent sessions** keep a chosen number of journeys active, starting another as one finishes.


If you’ve used JMeter, splitting workloads into[Thread Groups](https://jmeter.apache.org/usermanual/component_reference.html#Thread_Group) will feel familiar. k6 explains the difference between independent arrivals and workers that wait in its[open and closed workload models](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/concepts/open-vs-closed/) .


Load plans also support **Adaptive TPS** , which adjusts workers within a group’s budget to reach a request-rate target. **Traffic copies** and **recorded multiples** let you scale the workload you recorded.


You can combine these schedules with[chaos rules](https://speedscale.com/blog/scoped-chaos-rules-proxymock/) . For example, increase statement traffic and add dependency latency while keeping posting traffic steady. If the generator can’t start work on schedule, missed starts fail the run by default.


## Replay the whole user journey


Sometimes a single endpoint is enough. Other times, the transaction only makes sense after someone has logged in and looked up an account.


A session group selects recorded users whose journeys match your filter, then replays each complete journey. You can still measure just the transaction request within it.


The number of recorded users and the number active at once are separate settings. You might have 100 eligible users with ten journeys running at a time.


**Rotate** cycles through those users, **Sticky** prefers to reuse an available user, and **Once** runs each user exactly once. The same user never runs two journeys at the same time.


Increasing concurrency doesn’t create accounts. If you clone a journey, you need identity fields and transforms that produce accounts the app accepts. A new customer ID won’t provision a bank account for you.


For a closer look at how recorded sessions work, see[the Datadog Synthetics walkthrough](https://speedscale.com/blog/isolate-a-user-session-in-datadog-synthetics-with-proxymock/) .


## Decide what would fail the test


Here’s the banking test I’d start with: keep posting at two starts per second while statements ramp from five to twenty. During the final twenty seconds, require posting p95 response-header latency to stay below 500 milliseconds.


That goal applies to posting alone, during the busy part of the test. Set a minimum sample count, too. If there aren’t enough samples, the goal fails.


If you’ve used k6[thresholds](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/thresholds/) , the idea is similar. Here, the goal applies to a selected group of replayed requests and a time window.


The report shows planned starts, actual starts, HTTP attempts, failures and latency for each group. It also separates work finishing after the schedule ends. Successful HTTP responses alone don’t tell you whether the generator delivered the load you asked for.


We caught a reporting bug this way during development. The Kubernetes generator sent exactly 100 statement requests and 50 posting requests, but an older analyzer in staging dropped their throughput verdicts. The acceptance check failed because those results were missing.


## The mock surprised me


I expected mocking the statement dependency to make our local test loop faster. It didn’t.


Across[eight matched real and mock trials](https://speedscale.com/resources/load-plan-measurements/real-vs-mock-8-trials.json) , the median was 143.19 ms with the real local dependency and 149.46 ms with the mock. We timed resets, fixture discovery, complete sessions and checks against the bank’s request journal. Capture, process startup, cluster setup and uploads were excluded.


A[repeat with 30 matched pairs](https://speedscale.com/resources/load-plan-measurements/real-vs-mock-30-pairs.json) using the tagged engine told the same story. The real dependency had a 133.88 ms median and 136.90 ms p95. The mock came in at 137.35 ms and 140.41 ms, making its median 2.59% slower.


Another local test was sharing the host, so these numbers describe that comparison rather than a capacity benchmark.


What I got was a predictable dependency. With` proxymock` handling statement responses, the bank’s authentication, transaction handling and workload generator still ran for real. The bank’s own journal let us check what reached the app.


We also ran separate Kubernetes acceptance tests against the operator, generator and cloud reports. The local loop couldn’t tell us whether those components preserved the load plan and its results.


There’s more on choosing which dependencies to replace in[combining load tests with mocks](https://speedscale.com/blog/combining-load-tests-mocks/) .


## Try one load test with two workloads


Pick an endpoint your users depend on. Give it steady traffic and a latency goal. Then increase traffic to another endpoint that shares its database, cache or thread pool, and see what happens.


Use request groups to test individual endpoints. Use session groups when login, account identity and the order of requests matter.


The[sessions demo](https://github.com/speedscale/demo/tree/master/sessions-demo) includes the banking app, its statement dependency and both tests:


```text
cd   sessions-demo
PROXYMOCK_BIN  =  /absolute/path/to/proxymock   make   bank-load-workers
```


The[endpoint and session load plan guide](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/replay/endpoint-session-load-plans/) walks through both banking plans, the dashboard and Kubernetes setup. For more on replaying traffic in a cluster, see[Speedscale load testing](https://speedscale.com/features/load-testing/) and our[Kubernetes load testing guide](https://speedscale.com/blog/kubernetes-load-testing/) .


For the banking app, the result I want is straightforward: when statement traffic goes up, can people still post transactions within the latency limit?


## Frequently asked questions


### Can each endpoint have its own load schedule and latency goal?


Yes, with compatible load-plan components. Put the selected requests in separate groups, configure each schedule, and scope the latency goal and measurement window to the endpoint you care about. Require a minimum sample count and inspect delivery as well as latency. A configured target is not evidence that the generator delivered it.


### How do endpoint load and session replay differ?


A request-group arrival starts one selected request. A session-group arrival starts a complete recorded journey, which can include login and several endpoints. Session population, concurrent journeys, and starts per second are distinct settings. More workers do not create valid users or accounts; prepare identities and token correlation for the target environment.


### How do I know whether the app or the test harness is saturated?


Compare scheduled and actual starts, missed starts, completed requests, and latency while monitoring generator CPU, throttling, networking, and mock capacity. Check application and database metrics too. Repeat with more harness headroom while keeping the workload fixed. Generator saturation can distort latency, so a missed throughput target alone does not identify an application bottleneck.


Sources:[Endpoint and session load plans](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/replay/endpoint-session-load-plans/) ,[Generator sizing and bottlenecks](https://docs.speedscale.com/reference/generator-sizing-guide/) .
